memories-of-underdevelopment-1968.gazette: Newsreel is cut straight into the fiction: the Bay of Pigs footage, the October 1962 broadcasts, Havana as it stood while Alea was filming in it. Sergio watches from an apartment his family has already left for Miami, and the record keeps interrupting him. The crisis reaches him the way it reached everyone else on the island — over the radio, in real time.

funeral-parade-of-roses-1969.gazette: The bars of Shinjuku Ni-chōme supplied most of the cast, and Matsumoto stops the fiction cold to put a camera in front of them and ask about their own lives. The answers are their own, delivered in the rooms where they worked, and the crew's questions are left in. Nothing about the film asks to be taken as invention.

gimme-shelter-1970.gazette: The Maysles were already filming the 1969 tour when the free concert at Altamont Speedway, on 6 December, put a killing in front of their cameras. The finished film sits Jagger at a flatbed editing table, running the reel back frame by frame to find the knife and the gun in the crowd. The man who stabbed Meredith Hunter was tried and acquitted on the strength of that same footage.
gimme-shelter-1970.prism: Evidence and product are the same object here — the frames that decided a verdict are the frames that got a release, and the band that hired the security is the band paying for the edit. Jagger at the flatbed is the closest the film comes to a cross-examination, and nobody in that room is under oath.

the-wild-child-1970.gazette: Itard filed his reports on the boy taken out of the woods of Aveyron and delivered to the Paris institute for deaf-mutes, and Truffaut reads them aloud in the film, dated, in the first person. He also plays Itard. What the record documents is a physician charting progress in a child who never learned to speak.

the-sorrow-and-the-pity.gazette: Ophüls built four and a half hours out of interviews in and around Clermont-Ferrand — a schoolteacher, shopkeepers, a Frenchman who had fought in German uniform, Pierre Mendès France — set against wartime newsreel. It played in cinemas from 1971 and stayed off French television for a decade. The resistance myth it took apart had been state policy since the Liberation.

aguirre-the-wrath-of-god-1972.gazette: Ursúa's expedition set out down river in 1560 after El Dorado. Aguirre took it over, put his renunciation of Philip II in writing, and was dead in Venezuela within the year — all of that survives in the Spanish record. The diary Herzog frames the film with does not: Gaspar de Carvajal had gone down the Amazon two decades earlier, with someone else entirely.
aguirre-the-wrath-of-god-1972.prism: Reception has spent fifty years sorting the invented parts from the documented ones, which is a backhanded compliment to the fake diary — it looks exactly like the kind of source the conquest actually left behind. And the real Aguirre wrote his own account of himself; the film hands the narration to a priest instead.

day-for-night-1973.gazette: The title is a lighting trick — shoot in daylight, underexpose, filter, sell it as night — and the film is named for the craft it then spends two hours documenting. Truffaut set it at the Victorine studios in Nice and cast himself as the director, so the insurance, the schedule, the continuity notes and the cat that will not hit its mark all get screen time. People in the trade tend to quote it for the paperwork, not the romance.

the-exorcist-1973.gazette: The angiogram sequence was filmed in a working hospital with the radiologist and technicians playing themselves; Friedkin came out of documentary and shot the medicine that way. Jesuits advised on the rite, and two priests appear in the film as priests. The hardest reel to sit through is the one where nothing supernatural happens.

the-mother-and-the-whore-1973.gazette: Eustache wrote every line and had it delivered exactly as written — nothing in the three and a half hours is improvised, and almost all of it takes place in Paris cafés and one bed. The material came out of his own life closely enough that one of the women playing it had lived part of it with him. It is post-68 Paris talking itself hoarse, five years after everything was supposed to have changed.
the-mother-and-the-whore-1973.prism: The verbatim script is the trick: it plays like eavesdropping and it's dictation, which means every evasion in it was composed in advance. And the private life it draws on wasn't only his — someone it borrows from is there in frame, saying the lines.

the-spirit-of-the-beehive-1973.gazette: A village hall, a travelling projectionist and a print of Frankenstein make up the 1940 the film reconstructs, shot in a Castilian village while the man who won that war was still in power and still censoring. Erice worked on his six-year-old lead rather than with her: what Ana Torrent does in front of the monster is a reaction, not a performance. The house is lit through honeycomb glass.

lancelot-du-lac-1974.gazette: Functional armour, not costume armour — Bresson had it built to work, and then let the soundtrack be mostly that: hinges, buckles, hooves, a lance splitting. The tournament is cut almost entirely below the waist, legs and banners and horses passing the same patch of ground, which is what a man inside a helmet gets to see. The knights are played by people who were not actors.

scenes-from-a-marriage-1974.gazette: Bergman made it for Swedish television first, six episodes on 16mm with a crew small enough to fit inside the rooms, and cut it down for cinemas afterwards. There is little in it but two people at a table and a camera close enough to count the pauses. It went out an episode a week, and the country argued about it at the same interval.
scenes-from-a-marriage-1974.prism: The format is the argument: no job crisis, no money trouble, no children in the room — Bergman strips out everything a couple could blame and leaves them with each other. That's a realism contract only a certain class of marriage is in a position to sign.

the-conversation-1974.gazette: Coppola brought in a working San Francisco surveillance man as consultant, and the rigs in the Union Square sequence — the shotgun mics on the rooftops, the operator with the bag — are how the job was actually done. Murch built the sound so the audience does Caul's work, running the same few seconds of tape until the words change meaning. The script was written before Watergate; the film opened in the year Nixon resigned.

dersu-uzala-1975.gazette: Arseniev surveyed the Ussuri taiga for the Russian army in the first decade of the century and published what he had written down, the Nanai hunter who guided him included. Kurosawa shot it there with a Soviet crew, across more than a year of real seasons in the same forest. Dersu was a real man, and by the account his surveyor left, he was killed in 1908 for the rifle he had been given.

dog-day-afternoon-1975.gazette: On 22 August 1972 two men walked into a Chase branch in Gravesend to rob it and were still inside some fourteen hours later, with the street outside full of police, television crews and a crowd. Lumet shot on a Brooklyn block and kept the part the cameras made possible: the robber working the audience, and the chant of Attica, eleven months after the prison. The younger man was shot dead at Kennedy Airport that night; the other went to prison and wrote from there that the film had it wrong.
dog-day-afternoon-1975.prism: A robbery that turned into a broadcast is the whole event — Wojtowicz played to the crowd because the crowd was live, and the film can only be this accurate because the news feed was already rolling. What the coverage flattened at the time the movie largely leaves flattened: the surgery he said he was raising the money for belonged to a person the papers would not name correctly.
